Fourth, geometric incompatibility: curved plate margins force localized shear zones.

## Types of Plate Boundaries

Earthquakes do not happen everywhere in equal numbers. They cluster along plate boundaries. The key point: earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions.

## Plate Speeds in Action
Plate speeds matter because they set how fast strain builds at plate boundaries. The material gives two worked examples. The Pacific Plate moves northwest relative to the North American Plate at about 5 cm per year. The Nazca Plate subducts, meaning it sinks beneath another plate, under South America at about 8 cm per year.
These fast rates explain the high frequency of large earthquakes along the Circum-Pacific 'Ring of Fire.' Faster motion means strain accumulates quickly, so large events happen more often.
Earthquake depth also follows a pattern. Shallow events, at 10 km depth or less, dominate divergent ridges and transform faults. Intermediate to deep events, from 30 to 300 km, occur in the Wadati-Benioff zone of subducting slabs.
At a convergent margin, the seismic cycle has stages. In the interseismic stage, a locked zone accumulates strain over decades to centuries. In the coseismic stage, sudden slip releases the stored elastic energy in seconds to minutes. In the postseismic stage, afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation redistribute stress over months to years. A preseismic stage may show precursory signals such as foreshocks or slow slip.
For hazard assessment, seismic gap theory says that segments which have not ruptured in a full cycle are candidates for future large events. GPS and InSAR measure plate-scale velocities in cm per year to refine coupling models.

## The Seismic Cycle at a Convergent Margin
At a convergent margin, one plate slides beneath another. The seismic cycle is the repeating pattern of strain building, sudden slip, and slow recovery. It has four stages, listed here in cycle order.

Stage 3 – Postseismic: afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation redistribute stress over months to years. Stage 4 – Preseismic: possible precursory signals, such as foreshocks and slow slip.

Intermediate to deep events, 30–300 km, occur in the Wadati-Benioff zone of subducting slabs. A typical subduction earthquake at 30 km depth releases energy from both crustal bending and slab dehydration.
These ideas feed hazard assessment. Seismic gap theory says that segments which have not ruptured in a full cycle are candidates for future large events. GPS and InSAR monitor plate-scale velocities, in cm per year, to refine coupling models.

## Hazard Assessment Tools
This skill is a checklist for judging earthquake hazard at a plate boundary. First, identify the boundary type: divergent, transform, or convergent. The type controls where earthquakes happen and how deep they are.
Second, get the relative plate speed in cm per year from global models such as MORVEL or NUVEL-1A. Fast rates mean strain builds quickly. The Pacific Plate moves about 5 cm yr⁻¹ relative to North America, and the Nazca Plate subducts beneath South America at about 8 cm yr⁻¹. These rates explain the frequent large earthquakes of the Circum-Pacific Ring of Fire.
Third, map earthquake depths. Shallow events (≤ 10 km) dominate ridges and transform faults. Intermediate to deep events (30–300 km) occur in the Wadati-Benioff zone of a subducting slab. Depth tells you the seismogenic thickness, the depth range that can break in an earthquake.
Fourth, evaluate coupling and seismic gap status. A seismic gap is a segment that has not ruptured in a full earthquake cycle, so it is a candidate for a future large event. GPS and InSAR measure plate-scale velocities to refine coupling models, and depth distribution informs likely rupture extent and tsunami potential.

This skill is a four-step checklist for evaluating earthquake hazard in a region. It is meant as a quick reference during lectures and problem sessions.
Step 1: Identify the plate boundary type for the region of interest. The boundary type (for example, subduction or transform) sets the character of the hazard.
